entities.summary:
Calvisia Domitia Lucilla Minor (b. c. 100 CE, Sinuessa), a prominent figure of the Antonine Dynasty in Roman Italy, played a crucial, albeit often indirect, role in the economic and political stability of the Roman Empire through her immense personal wealth and strategic familial connections. As the mother of Emperor Marcus Aurelius and wife of Marcus Annius Verus, she exemplified the power and influence wielded by aristocratic Roman women who, despite lacking formal political office, shaped imperial succession and maintained vast financial networks across the Mediterranean. Her landholdings and commercial enterprises, particularly in the production of olive oil, positioned her as a significant economic force in the provinces of Baetica and Africa Proconsularis, underpinning Rome's critical food supply chains.

Lucilla's economic activities were extensive, including the ownership of substantial olive groves and associated production facilities (officinae) in regions vital for Rome’s agricultural output. Inscriptions from amphorae stamps (e.g., 'C.D.L.') found throughout the Roman world, particularly along the Tiber in Rome, attest to the vast scale of her olive oil exports. This mercantile engagement was not merely personal enrichment; it was integral to the provisioning of Rome itself, a city reliant on massive imports. Her management of these estates and commercial ventures demonstrated a sophisticated understanding of Roman imperial logistics and trade, contributing directly to the welfare and provisioning of the urban populace and the military.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Calvisia Domitia Lucilla's vast economic power and strategic familial connections directly supported the imperial household and contributed to the stability of the Antonine Dynasty, notably through her son, Emperor Marcus Aurelius. Her extensive commercial operations helped provision the Roman capital and military, demonstrating the vital role of aristocratic women in the Roman economy.
